nameStory: True indigo gets its name from being one of the original and most prized sources of deep blue indigo dye, which has been treasured for thousands of years. The word 'indigo' comes from the Greek 'indikon,' meaning 'from India,' where this plant was first cultivated commercially for its incredible blue coloring power.
description: True indigo is a bushy, upright shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall with delicate, feathery compound leaves. This tropical plant from the bean family produces small pink to reddish flowers in slender clusters and develops short, curved seed pods. In New England, it's extremely rare and would only survive as an annual or in very protected locations, making any sighting quite special.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-13 small, oval leaflets arranged along a central stem like a feather - soft to touch and bright green

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink, red, or salmon-colored flowers clustered in narrow spikes that emerge from leaf joints - flowers are pea-like in shape

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, branching shrub with thin, flexible stems that have a somewhat woody texture at the base

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Short, curved brown pods about half an inch long that split open to reveal small, dark seeds

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, green to reddish stems with a slightly ridged texture and fine, short hairs that feel fuzzy when rubbed

habitat: In its native range, true indigo thrives in warm, well-drained soils and full sun. In New England, any occurrence would likely be in the warmest, most protected microclimates - perhaps near heated buildings, in urban heat islands, or as cultivated specimens in botanical gardens.

seasonality.spring: Young plants would emerge late in spring after soils warm thoroughly, developing their characteristic compound leaves first.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and flowering season, with pink flower clusters appearing and small curved pods beginning to develop in the warmest months.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open to release seeds, while the entire plant begins to decline with cooler temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors - any plants would be killed by the first frost.

funFact: A single true indigo plant can produce enough dye to color several yards of fabric that deep, rich blue that was once more valuable than gold - so precious that it sparked international trade wars and colonial fortunes!
confusionNotes: With only 2 sightings recorded in New England, confusion is unlikely, but it might be mistaken for other legumes with compound leaves like wild senna or lead plant. The key difference is true indigo's distinctive pink-to-red flowers and its extremely rare occurrence in our region.
contextualKnowledge: True indigo is historically significant as the source of natural indigo dye before synthetic dyes were invented in the 1800s. It was so economically important that entire colonial economies, including parts of South Carolina, were built around its cultivation.
compareHints: As the only Indigofera species recorded in New England, true indigo is most similar to other legumes with compound leaves, but differs from native species like wild senna by having pink rather than yellow flowers and much smaller leaflets. Unlike our common native legumes, it lacks the robust cold tolerance needed for New England's climate.
